review:
Oh boy, this game.

Well, it's fun, the combat is very fast paced and fun, you can do a lot of moves with your skills and magic and abilities, you can combine them or charge them for a more powerful attack. 

This game is HUGE, the map is VERY HUGE, there are a lot of dungeons and there is like 300 or 400 side quests to be done, but  it is very unlikely that you will want to do every single one, you see, most of them, most of the quests are like the generic MMO quests (grab question with NPC > kill x things > collect x things > go back to NPC), but there is a lot of side quests very well done and with a nice story. 

Play this game on HARD, because even on HARD it will be kinda easy, seriously, you will only face a challenge if you decide to fight more than 6 enemies (of your LEVEL - the ones with the name in YELLOW) at once or an enemy with an ORANGE or RED name.

There are a lot of things to say about this game, but let me give you some tips that won't ruin your fun.

If you want to kill enemies with one or two hits, pick  BLACKSMITH and JEWELCRAFTING skill to level up, you will be able to craft your own gear, but you can make some GODLY gear, like, you can gain +60% DAMAGE with FIRE DAMAGE and LIFE LEECH and an insane amount of ARMOR, you will never die, really, it will look like GOD MODE. If you wanna some challenge in the fights and if you wanna use the nice sets and unique gear that you will find in the game (the uniques and set items are way more nice than the crafted ones, they are very stylish and have some nice stats and their own lore/description, but they don't have stats so powerful like the crafted gear), don't level up BLACKSMITHING, go for JEWELCRAFTING (to sell the jewels) and MERCANTILE so you can make a lot of money (i ended up with 12 millions GOLD and wasn't even in the end of the game, i had like 25 hours or more till the final boss).

Try to acquire the DLCs, Ded Kel and Teeth of Naros, they are very nice and the Ded Kel can grant you some nice things, like, you can acquire the best items for crafting (the FLAWLESS components, they grant insane stats for crafted gear) and a lot of uniques and set items (set gear) for FREE (the components are not free, but the gear that one NPC search for you is free), a NPC will get them for you.

Choose well the color of the eye of your character, you won't be able to change this after, only hair and jewels and tattoos once you gain your own house (there is like 3 or 4 houses only for your character in the game).

Try to do all the faction quests, they give you nice rewards and you end up meeting new NPCs and enjoying the stories.

Try to level up the DETECT HIDDEN skill, it will help you a lot. Don't bother, seriously, don't bother with LOCKPICKING and PERSUASION (PERSUASION can be nice if you really want some more dialogues, but it is not necessary), LOCKPICKING is useless, really, you will find some hard chests to lockpick, but after 3 or 4 lockpicks (and you will find and will be able to afford a lot of those lockpicks) you will end up opening the chests without problem. Try to level up DISPELLING, it will help you on magic chests and will prevent you for being cursed (curses can't be removed without a HEALER, and you will be forced to travel to a city or village to lift the curse, otherwise you can continue exploring, but some curses can make your character very vulnerable, very weak).

Try to read all the books you find, really, they can give you a nice understanding of the lore and they have some very interesting information, also, some of them are hilarious.

***If you want more challenge, you can try to use the YSA mod, it is a mod to be used with the Cheat Engine program, it changes the game to be way more challenging, i've never used but a lot of people said that it is very well done and you can choose what to use (like, you can disable the way your character receives damage [with the mod your character receives 2x or 3x more damage from the enemies] or the XP gain [experience is reduced by default with the mod]). ***


There is lot of more i would like to say, but i don't remember everything now. I hope this review help you.

Thanks for reading.

Get this game. You get 60-90 hours of gameplay for the price. Few single player games can say that.

[u]The good[/u]

Massive game world, even without the DLCs
Bright and colourful environments, jungles, deserts, forests etc
Awesome combat and spell effects
Great combat/magic specialisation
Loads quickly, runs fast
Hundreds of quests
Excellent crafting
Crafting materials don't count as inventory items
Better than reasonable music
Lots of background lore and information
80+ hours of gameplay with the DLCs
It's an addictive game, you want to keep going and see what's next
Loot out the wazoo

[u]The bad[/u]

Camera goes all screwy during combat
Can't look fully up or down
Some very average dungeon designs, lots of near-identical looking places
Lots of backtracking
Lots of step and fetch it/fedex type quests
Some of the voice acting is average
RNG at work with chests and loot drops in general. Get epic loot in easy chests, get trash in very hard chests etc
There's arguably too much loot in the game, but that's a minor complaint

Underrated story-driven RPG (console port)

Pros:
[list]
    [*]Fun rogue/mage hybrid, good stealth.
    [*]Good map and dungeon design.
    [*]Loot feels worthwhile.
    [*]Every quest is part of a story arc.
    [*]Good world-building, plenty of details.
    [*]Decisions have an effect on the game.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*]Block/stagger mechanic is over-used.
    [*]Poor PC controls (much better with a controller)
    [*]Cannot zoom out (can use WideScreenFixer)
    [*]Only supports XBox controllers (can use x360ce)
[/list]

Game-breaking stuff:
[list]
    [*]Play the game on Hard, otherwise it's too easy. There's an achievement for it, too.
    [*]Don't enter new areas (loading screen) too early; new zones are locked to your current level.
    [*]Avoid bonus XP, since it will over-level you too quickly.
    [*]Don't max out Blacksmithing, it will quickly make all loot redundant.
    [*]Limit the number of health potions you carry :P
[/list]

If you're a PC gamer, you might be inclined to try to dodge everything.
This can work in late-game, but early on you will need to block more than you dodge.

Things you need to know:
[list]
    [*]Block early, block often. It's a console thing. This alone will make the game 50% easier.
    [*]Be aggressive. The more you hit enemies, the less they hit you (because they are staggered)
    [*]Don't try to dodge small melee attacks. If you can see the attack, it's too late to dodge in most cases.
    [*]Dodge is for boss attacks and blinking through enemies. Especially trolls.
    [*]You can block (or riposte) later than you can dodge.
    [*]You can block magic, and wolves.
    [*]Chakrams don't interrupt attacks. Use daggers for that, or stay mid-range.
    [*]Daggers are awesome.
[/list]

I am nearly 200 hours into this game (80% of the time being in the last four years), I have derived nothing but enjoyment from it. Depsite the fact that the game DOES have an end, the amount of content stuffed into this one game is staggering. Of the 194 hours played on my profile, 100 hours is just ONE playthrough, completing all the sidequests I could find and immersing myself in everything the game had to offer. 

Bottom line: if you want a game that you can play for 100+ hours on a single playthrough and you love the medieval-fantasy, magic and mystery genre with an action RPG fighting system then this is the game for you.

To sum it up: I paid 9.99 for this game,  and I felt I've gotten my money's worth, easily.  

Overall Impressions: For looks and general feel - in one sentence, I'd describe it as the b**tard child of Torchlight and Skyrim.  It feels like it has borrowed something from both.  It feels like a game that was, at one point, to be grander and bigger than it ended up being; potentially interesting lore feels a bit stilted and half-told  (or, oddly sometimes OVERtold) at times, the music is occasionally good but most often forgettable.  If you've ever been really taken somewhere else by an amazing track - some of the Skyrim music, or the Nagrand themes from Warcraft, if I name two personal favourites -  you will not find that experience replicated here musically.  I found the starting area the worst as it seemed to be very limited in tracks - once I moved out into the world more, things seemed to improve.

While it's less cartoon-like and lighthearted than Torchlight, it is far more static, less vibrant and fluid than Skyrim - but there are aspects to both that came to mind while playing this.

Cinematics are limited, as are camera angles, and movement over the map in general - designated "jump down spots", inability to climb over/around objects, etc. will be obvious to you if you're the kind of person who killed mounts in Skyrim until you modded them to be invulnerable, because you're going to go over the mountain YOUR way, and that's that.

In fact, you won't be on a mount at all - but in compensation, the fast travel feature is made available very early on, and the map fills up with quite a few waypoints.

 As a single-player game, it's MMO roots - while generally hidden - do show from time to time, if only in the vague sense of feeling like the world feels a bit -emptier- than one might expect.   There's thankfully a dearth of overly "grindy" quests (kill 100 of this to get 50 of that), but there's also skills that feel fairly usless (crafting gems, more on that below), and make you wonder if, had this been an MMO, had there been high-end/group content, they'd have become more beneficial.

More specific comments/aspects:

General gameplay - the game is stable enough, but I have found more than a handful of buggy quest issues - quests that don't complete correctly and can't be fixed without a rollback to an earlier save. Items that when used, don't spawn the map point related to them, little things like that.

However, unless you're dead set on a particular item or quest, you will find levelling in this game so fast that you WILL outlevel quests and gear very easily.  Particularly if you tend to build up your fate bar quickly, for XP gains, and/or drink experience potions - it's going to fly by.

Combat - for me it's PRO OR CON, depending on what you want: combat is fun - flashy, satisfying - but I definitely would not call it challenging. The visuals are entertaining, and at times funny, and while I appreciate a game that makes you AIM attacks and spells properly, I also feel you pretty much hit the ground overpowered (at least on normal).  On the upside, being able to respec and play with talent combos is a no-brainer, and only a minor investment even fairly early on in the levels.  Improvements to the character and various perks are generously offered through quest lines, challenges, discoveries, etc.

Loot - You'll end up with so many epics and set pieces that you will be bored with it after a point.  However, said loot is not all it's cracked up to be (see notes below on talents).  Weapon choices are many, loot is generous, and with the freewheeling respec potential via the fateweavers, you can easily change the entire path your character is taking anytime you see fit, just to try out something cool that's dropped.

Talents -  To some extent, the talents you choose can cause the loot aspect to really fall short, because if you choose to skill up blacksmithing and gemcrafting as early as I did, it only takes a few lucky salvages for components before you're going to make gear for yourself that far, far outshines the very best drops you get, the vast majority of the time, and since there's no point in the game where you can disenchant purple/epic or yellow/set items, much of that ends up in your stash, or vendored.   You can name the gear you craft, which is occasionally entertaining.

Socketing gems is something they obviously intended the player to do, as beyond a certain level, socketed items drop regularly, but even there, no item that's dropped with open sockets has come close to crafted gear, since - once skilled up - you can use gems as part of the blacksmithing process. 

Detect hidden is surprisingly lucrative, leading to extra gold - but also stashes of loot, secret doors, and ultimately opening up items on the map that would take time to hunt down otherwise.

One aspect that I DID find fun, and a bit more interesting (having played a rogue-type character in multiple games for years), is the stealth ability - without resorting to invisibility potions, you are forced - especially until you're skilled up - to pay real attention to the direction in which your target is facing, the patterns in which they move or change direction, etc. 

In short - it's easy to learn, easy to play, generally smooth, fun to look at, and (in a good way), easy to put down. I've no regrets about buying it on sale, and while I'm not sure it screams "second playthrough", I can only give it a thumbs up for a generally entertaining - if imperfect - rpg experience.

I hope that's useful to someone. Recommended, yes.

This is one of the best RPG I've ever played with a few minor problems.

 First the graphics are really pretty good. 

 The story line tells an interesting story.

 One of the best things is the way it alllows you, at the start, to set up the character you want to play. Most RPG games will let you do this, but this one has a really nice set up to let you do this with either male or female. Also, you aren't done there you can change some of those settings like hair style & color, and other things as you work your way thru the game. 

 I also really like the way my X-Box 360 controller worked with this game. In a lot of games, you find yourself having to reset all the buttons etc so you could use them. I didn't have that problem here. The settings are well done and once you get used to the settings they are easy to use. I also noted that dodging was REALLY dodging and in line with what you did with the controller. If you wanted to hit someone and then turn quickly to shoot at some one else you could and your character would carry out that action, not pause or do something you didn't expect. Also the action was smooth too and walking or running were set up right and you could explore easily and not be forced to run all the time.  The other good thing I noted was the attention to menus when using the X-Box 360 controller. These were set to mirror either a KB/mouse or controller when showing what button or key did what. The only thing I noticed, like most newer games, it can switch on you if you are using the controller and switch to the mouse to do select a menu option. (I didn't have any trouble with it myself.)

 Game play was overall very nice.  There are a lot of side quests and you can spent a large amount of time roaming around and there are a few that can be failed if you're not careful. 

 Like all good games there are some things that aren't so great.

 The leveling up system only goes to level 40 and you don't really get to use the many skills that you can get, but even this has some good points. You get a number of ways to get you skills and can decided how to set up the talents your character will specialize in, even if you end at 40 with no where to go. This does have some interesting side effects like having your character being a bit over powering as you revisit certain early areas again . 

 Overall, I was very impressed by this game and liked it very much.  I can heartily recommend this game and think you will find in very intertaining to play.

For the record, I also own Kingdoms of Amalur for the Xbox 360 and PS3 and have beat it five times. I have played as every class (warrior, mage, archer/stealth) and mixtures of the three. Although I was excited for this game before its release, Kingdoms of Amalur released in February 2012, mere months after Skyrim. I'd spent hundreds of hours in Skyrim by that point and loved it to pieces. I figured Kingdoms of Amalur would be a disappointment in comparison.

Other than being action RPGs, the two games aren't really comparable. I love Kingdoms of Amalur, but its issues are deep and teeter on the edge of game-breaking sometimes. This is the only game 38 Studios published before their bankruptcy kerfuffle. As a debut game, Kingdoms is fantastic, yet it also bears a lot of flaws that seasoned development teams often conquer in subsequent games.

In Kingdoms, you play as a character who died and is brought back to life. The story branches out from there, touching upon themes having to do heavily with fate, unraveling it, destinies, and so forth. To be honest, even though I've beaten the game multiple times, I have little memory of the story. It is forgettable, and as a person who doesn't believe in fate/destiny, it's simply uninteresting. Kingdoms has a problem with forgettable stories, lore, and characters. I saw another review comparing it to an MMO, and the comparison is fair. I'm someone who goes into an RPG hoping to get obsessed with lore; in Skyrim, for example, I keep libraries of in-game texts and I actually read them. Here? I tried, and I just can't get into it. Historical events, people, and wars are vaguely explained and low on detail, forcing you to only stick to the present. Nearly all NPCs in the game are lackluster. When I come across an NPC who manages to spark my interest, it surprises me.

So why in the world do I like this game enough to keep coming back? The gorgeous, unique fantasy world and ridiculously fun combat. Kingdoms of Amalur isn't the best-looking graphically; the character designs are often hideous (clunky animations in facial expressions often lead to unintentionally hilarious or creepy conversations), and if you walk closely to anything you might start to see its flaws. But on the whole, they did a fabulous job of creating a world that feels enormous despite its straightforward map-to-map pathways, and the locations are gorgeous. From gigantic forests where the trees assault the skies to rolling plains to the canyons of a desert, this game is a feast for the eyes and the world is simply fun to explore. Never before have I experienced a fantasy game like this that feels whimsical without being innocent (the enemy designs can sometimes be eerie, and blood spills frequently in combat). Amalur feels unique in this aspect; the world is so gorgeous and colorful that a lot of times I'll feel like playing just to look at it.

As for the combat, it's ridiculously easy. But you will look and feel like a badass no matter how you play. My least favorite play style was as a two-handed weapon warrior, because combat is slow and leaves you vulnerable to the ramming attacks of low-level enemies like wolves, brownies, etc. Still, the combat was fluid and beautiful. My favorite way to play is with faeblades and chakrams; seriously, at least try using chakrams once. These weapons are gorgeous, elementally-imbued, and sweep through enemies and the environment alike to where nothing can touch you. Even on hard difficulty, this game is a cakewalk. But at least it's a ton of fun as you play.

A few other tidbits: the quests and enemies are unfortunately low on variety. Even when you join the Travelers (a thieves' guild, essentially), you'll find yourself completing clear-out-a-dungeon-and-kill-a-boss type quests rather than stealing more often than not. It seems like the developers tried to emulate other games with factions (like Elder Scrolls) but just did it poorly; Amalur has varied factions, of which you can join them all, but their questlines are lackluster and all start to mimic one another. Enemy designs are pathetically few and far between; you might make it to a new area and think, "Oh! I'll start facing new enemies now!" Ehh, unlikely. Going from the forests to the deserts only netted me a few new elven enemy types; all the creature enemies stayed the same. And if you're heading toward a climax battle and think you'll get a unique enemy type, I have bad news for you: 9 times out of 10, it'll just be a human/elf who calls themselves a special name, and they won't be harder to beat than anyone else.

Kingdoms of Amalur also suffers from weird glitches and game-breaking bugs, one of which happened to me while playing the Dead Kel quests from the DLC on Steam. There's a mission where you have to run out of a collapsing cavern. I did so just to find my companion was stuck behind the rubble. There was no fast travel or way off the beach, so I reloaded just to come across the same thing. Lo and behold, the only way to fix the glitch was to restart the quest. The only other save I had was an autosave, so I lost 40 hours of gameplay progress. Basically, always keep at least two saves: one where you're in a safe place, and another for more recent gameplay. Amalur's glitches are rarely foreseeable, so you'll need a save when you least expect it.

All in all, I really like this game, but I want to love it. I wish 38 Studios had survived past Amalur and went on to grow from this experience, because underneath all the grime of rookie mistakes and uninteresting lore, there's a great game here. For a debut game, Amalur is an amazing effort. Had 38 Studios learned from its flaws and went on to create a sequel, I honestly could see their games going head-to-head with the Elder Scrolls installments and other mainstay RPGs. Unfortunately, their bankruptcy lost them this perfect opportunity, but we will always have Amalur. It's unique, it's troubled, it's sometimes frustrating, yet always beautiful. I'd give Kingdoms of Amalur a 6.5/10. At its best, it's higher; at its worst, it would be lower. Either way, it shouldn't be missed.

To be honest, when I bought the game I wasn't expecting much from this game. The screenshots looked nice and I am a huge RPG fan. So I bought it when it was on one of those typical Valve Season Sales.

This game is just great. It entertained me over 80 hours (well perhaps about 75 hours, the rest of my gameplay is menu idleing while reading guides or wiki). I saw many reviews comparing this with Skyrim, but be honest, they are very different.

Soundtrack is very nice. Background music gives great atmosphere, but sadly there are a lot of soundbugs. I didn't hear any background music in the last 20 hours of gameplay. Sometimes sound of my characters battle voices and those of my weapons disappear. Only fix I managed to think about was restarting the game.
The voice acting was nice. Although there are not that many voice actors, but they were doing a good job.

You can develop your character in different ways. You can chose between three different skill trees, basicly that is the decision between Knight, Rogue and Sorcerer. But you can play any combination of those as well. Your skill tree will determine what weapons you will use. I played with the Rogue skill tree because I like stealthy approaches, and the dagger and faeblades you find are really nice and very fast. Great in combination with a bow for range attacks.

You can make tons of side quests and task. After completing the game and both DLCs I managed to complete over 200 quests (including the main quest). 

Combat is very repetitive. When you know how it works, it gets very very easy and you will fight almost the same every time. I played the game on hard. The first 10 levels were hard, because of bad equipment and stupidity ;) But after that it was very easy. Maybe I died 20 times during the remaing 30 levels. 

Very nice was the fact, that NPCs you have to follow or are your companions don't run slower than you. They run at least as fast as you, sometimes even a little faster, but they are waiting if you get too far away. 

The only thing I really hated in this game was the camera. You cannot control the FOV. It adjust automatically to your current situation. Zooms out when there is an enemy far away. Gets closer if not. But sometimes this stupid camera drops below earth and all you see is dirt.
Or in cutscenes you will see just a wall or a shoulder of a total different NPCs

All in all a very nice RPG. Go get it when it is on sale. Take your time doing all side quests and you will be entertained for a long time.

This game belong in the pantheon of the greatest RPGs ever created!

The combat is pretty much Fable, Skyrim & God of War put into 1 game with a wonderful execution, the most enjoyable combat system that I have ever come across.

The world is huge and encourages you to explore it - there is a lot of lore present & quite a lot of interesting characters too. Also, the characters have a LOT to say, and it seems that every voice (which are a lot) are all different & it brings out a lot of immersion. A lot of variety in the areas you can visit too, you have deserts, plains, marshes, canyons and what not.

Almost nothing bad about this game, perhaps sometimes a bit texture pop-in, some boring fetch quests & characters that look-a-like, but the story is thick & it has literally 1000s of side-quests. You can buy houses, explore big cities, craft & more! Everything you want in a RPG!

It has a great ton of customization that allows you to change your skills & magic abilities on the fly, always be able to go with per example a Templar - using Magic & Heavy armor, or a Sorcerer, fully magic specced with robes & chakrams (Xena's weapons!) or a Thief, wielding light weapons with hints of magic - it is literally ALL possible!

There are many weapons too, Daggers, Bows, Fae Blades, Greatswords, Hammers, Sceptres, Staffs, Chakrams, and more that I cannot remember. It has any weapon you could think of in an  - and I did not even mention the magical abilites which are very numerous & work well together.

It also has a GREAT crafting mechanic that will have you searching all corners of the world for things to use, and as I said, it encourages it. Combined with the crafting mechanic itself is also sagecrafting - that allows you to create gems to use with equipment to enhance stats.

All in all, this is probably one of the best RPGs that I have ever played. 
It's a truly, really commendable game that every RPG lover should play!

Personal score: 9/10

What can I say about Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning?  It is an absolute and criminal shame that the company who put this game together dissolved before they could make a sequel.  The story line is decadent and entertaining, and the world has been robbed of a beautiful and engaging series by virtue of developers' bankruptcy.  Still, the only extant offering in the Kingdoms of Amalur series is definitely worth the price to play.  The game devs did not reinvent the wheel with regards to the RPG genre, but their ascendency comes from the wholly customizable class system.  Ever feel limited by the restrictive class system of other games?  Ever feel like your plate-wearing badass would also have access to sneaky, sneaky rogue tactics unavailable to your class?  Ever wonder if your mage would be just as adept at wielding a swords as at wielding magicks?  KoA allows you that opportunity and more with an imaginative and unique system that rewards your playstyle, whatever that might be, and if at anytime you regret your choice, just visit one of the many fateweavers in the game and change it all, for a token sum of coin of course.  Equally inventive are the skills, which are accessible regardless what "class" you've rolled.  All skills have utility: Alchemy makes potions ranging from health and mana to enchancing various types of damage done or reducing that received, blacksmithing creates armor and weaponry for every build, sagecrafting shapes gems to enhance your gear further, and those are just the tip of the iceburg.  Persuasion is decidedly worth the investment, but lockpicking is not, as only a skill point or two will carry you through the game, particularly as lockpicks are plentiful and the minigame is not difficult.  Speaking of difficulty, anyone just picking up the game would be well served to play it on the hardest difficulty setting; I was advised by a review to do so and never regretted it, as few of the encounters will shred your nerves, even on the hard.  If you want hard, go play Dark Souls.  If you want a fun take that shows the potential of what role playing games truly could be, try KoA.  This game is vast, with tons of quests and things to do in Amalur, helping the good people (or not, if you so choose).  I've spent over 200 hours in the game thus far, and there's plenty to indulge your completionist side.  Right now I'm seeking out the few remaining achievements after my first full play through.  The ending was a little lackluster, as though they ran out of time and money to finish the game properly, but the journey itself was rewarding.  Bottom line, for what it's likely to cost you to acquire this game, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a steal, but the real theft is that it's the only one of its line.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning™[/b] is a highly underrated, and truly epic, action-RPG.  Boasting hours and hours of content, it is loaded with a rich narrative and plenty of lore aspects to intrigue the fantasy buff in you.  It also has great RPG elements that will keep you striving to evolve your character. So if you enjoy that type of thing, and want to get immersed in a humongous game, then you should give this some consideration.  

The graphics are absolutely charming; and the gameworld is massive, variable, and captivating. It is very fun to explore the environments in search of loot and lore.  The controls are fluid and intuitive, and the combat is exciting and flexible. And the whole experience flows very naturally, so it is the type of game that is easy to get caught up in for hours on end.

There are tons of things to do and places to explore.  There is also a myriad of lore in the game and many NPCs to have extensive dialogues with. If you enjoy delving deep into the worlds of fantasy games, you’ll have plenty to work with.  There is also a huge variety of different enemies to vanquish, so your bloodlust should be satiated as well.  There are plenty of levels to be gained, abilities to be learned, items to loot, and armor sets to (try to) complete.  And there are over 200 quests, or far more if you pick up the DLC.  In short: it is undeniably an RPG of epic proportions. Moreover, considering it can easily last 100+ hours, the developers did a good job diversifying the content so it doesn’t grow too stale towards the end.

One exceptionally cool feature of the game is that you can freely respec as often as you want and change between mage, warrior, and rouge classes (or cross-class combinations thereof).  This helps keep things fresh through the lengthy campaign, and prevents you from having to pick a single playstyle for the entire game.

There are also a couple of DLC campaigns available for [b]Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning™[/b]. They are both quite lengthy and add a very large amount of content to the experience. I definitely recommend picking up the whole package, however be prepared for a game that will take about 150 hours for completionists.

So [b]Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning™[/b] is undeniably epic, massive, and downright fun.  If you enjoy huge RPGs like [i]Skyrim[/i] or [i]Dragon Age: Origins[/i] then you will probably enjoy this, perhaps lesser known, but similar, game.

A forgotten relic of when games were games, Kingdoms of Amalur is like the lovechild of Fable and Skyrim.

The game plays very much like Fable: block, dodge, primary weapon, secondary weapon, and a modifier key for magic on the face buttons. Easy to use and highly intuitive. There are a plethora of weapons to choose from, depending on your gameplay style and which class or classes you choose to pursue, ranging from fast, low damage knives that allow stealth kills, to ranged staves and sceptres for elemental damage, to slow and wide-reaching melee for tanking. The game even facilitates specific multi-class builds, giving you immense freedom for choosing how you want to play and progress.

Unlike Fable, this game takes itself and its high-fantasy world seriously, including plenty of lore books and a massive world to explore, like an Elder Scrolls game. There are amusing characters and dialogue here and there, but as is with most high-fantasy settings, you will mostly be encountering and tackling racism and religion throughout, which I find to be both compelling and original in its execution. Despite the map being huge, the world is broken up into "pods" of land, which allow you to fully explore an area before moving on to the next via various load-free 'corridors', which I find far more compelling than a gigantic, generic map like Just Cause, particularly when it is very focused on the single player experience of your journey.

In short, this is a sadly overlooked gem of RPGs, offering easy gameplay and deep immersion.

Kingdoms of Amalur is a open(ish) world, 3rd person roleplaying game where you play as a fateless hero who has resurrected from the dead with the help from a gnomish invention called the well of souls. You are quickly thrown into the action and for the most of the game, you try to figure out who you were before you died while also helping in the war against the armies of the fae king Gadflow. 

I will be making some comparisons to the game Skyrim in this review, as they are very similar games. And since Skyrim is such a well known game, most people reading this will have an idea what i'm talking about.

+PROS+
+The absolute biggest compliment to this game is the combat. It's extremely smooth and responsive. It is in my opinion the strong foundation of the game. It does however have one flaw that I will mention in the CONS section.

+ While having lockpicking that's the exact same as in Skyrim, they also have the addition of dispelling. Which is a small minigame where you need to click at the correct time on runes while you are on a timer. This is far more difficult and dangerous than a lock. If you fail to dispell an item, it will explode and either curse you or deal alot of damage to you.

+ Every zone has lorestones. Lorestones are blue stones who tell a small story when you interact with them. They can be rhymes, stories of the zone, some lore about the world or information about people. If you find and interact with all the lorestones in an area, you get a permanent buff. Like extra health, mana, goldfind etc. 

+ The three skilltrees you can choose from are rogue, warrior and mage. But you can also split your skill points into several trees. And for a small fee, you can reset your skillpoints to go a completely different route if you want to switch it up.

+ The game looks very beautiful visually.
+ Some really awesome cinematics.
+ You can earn several properties who has a shared storage box.
+ Many cutscenes where your character is present. Making it feel like you are actually part of the big story.
+ The music in this game is great, but there aren't that many tracks.
+ All quests are voicelined.
+ Several factions you can ally yourself with and do quite long questchains for.
+ Interesting story with equally interesting characters.
+ TONS of sidequests which will send you all over the world.
+ Cheap DLCs although in my opinion, only one of them is good.
+ Many different enemies who you should approach differently.

-CONS-
- As mentioned, the combat in the game has one giant flaw. Stagger.
See, when you attack an enemy, you set up an attack chain. The last attack of your attack chain will stagger the enemy, meaning it will get stunned, knocked down or disoriented for a few seconds. While they are staggered, you are free to keep attacking them without them being able to do anything in return, and your new stagger attack will hit them before they break out of their original stagger. This means the enemy can be permanently stunned while you hammer away at it.
This goes both ways though. Whenever you take damage, be it from a spell or sword, your spellcasting will be interupted and you will take half a second to recover. This may not sound like much, but if you are fighting 4-5 enemies and they attack you at different times, it might result in you being stunned the whole fight. I mostly found this as an issue on hard difficulty though.

- The carryweight system. If you are anything like me who likes to pick up anything you see, you are gonna hate this.
In Skyrim, you have a set amounts of weight you can carry, and items are weighted accordingly, like a piece of paper will be weightless, a bearhide will weigh 2 and a greatsword will weigh maybe 18. In Kingdoms of amalur however,  everything weighs the same, and you have an item cap instead. You can purchase bagspace in every major city, up to a total of 120.

- Some quests doesn't make sense at all. As an example, person A wanted me to kill person B. I went to person B and he told me that if I went back and killed person A instead, he would double my payment. Being a rogue, I figured I'd take him up on his offer and then stab him in the back as soon as he turned around. So I accepted, waited for him to turn around, backstabbed and killed him. The quest was then counted as FAILED. I went back to person A, but he had nothing to say to me anymore. So the questing system can be a bit black and white, and not very flexible.

- The world itself is very instanced. It is PACKED with invisible walls around edges and your character cannot jump. So it doesn't feel very smooth when you move around in the world.
- There were a few bugs with the music sometimes. Especially in the city Mel Senshir.
- The further you get in the game, there are less and less sidequests and interesting things in the world.
- The only DLC worth purchasing is Teeth of Naros. The others are empty and bad in my opinion.

If you like RPGs like Skyrim, then give this game a chance. If my CONS has made you doubt the game, get it on sale. It usually has a 75% discount during summer and winter sales. Although it has problems, it's an extremely solid game.

This is a highly underrated RPG that never got the credit it deserved due to some financial issues with the developer.

As others may have mentioned, the game plays a bit like a solo MMORPG. To elaborate: as you follow the main story lines, you'll find yourself going through different interconnected zones with central hubs full of quest givers. It's formulaic, but it really works. And while the game may appear to be a generic fantasy setting on the surface, it's at least a very well done one with its fair share of unique world building elements.

From a gameplay perspective, the combat is enjoyable and fast-paced. There are a limited number of skills and spells, but each weapon type has a distinct feel to it, much like Dark Souls, for instance. Grab a heavy two-handed sword and you'll find that each swing carries weight, and missing a blow can be costly due to the recovery time. Use quicker, one-handed weapons, on the other hand, and you can dance and dodge your way around enemies. There's also a timing-based parry system.

On the RPG/character building side, there's enough to keep you entertained (though it's certainly not an overly complicated system). The combat ability trees are simple enough (divided into your standard warrior/rogue/mage sections) with a few active abilities and several passive abilities. There's also a separate, non-combat skills section with things like stealth, sagecraft (enchanting, basically), blacksmithing, lockpicking, etc. If you're a min-maxxer, you may enjoy trying to max out all of these with limited points.

And just a few more things...

Pros:
* Beautiful soundtrack. It really gives you that faerie feel.
* Ditto for the graphics. They're just cartoonish enough to age well, and the dark art style fits the world perfectly.
* Rich variety in zones and plenty of unique storylines.
* So much content. Like, easily 100 hours per play-through in the base game if you're a completionist.

Cons:
* Difficulty scaling is an issue. Even on the hardest difficulty, the game becomes a cakewalk about 1/3 of the way in.
* Along those same lines: level scale locking in zones. The first time you enter a zone, the levels of every enemy in it are set. This means that you really have to finish each zone before moving on, otherwise you risk being overleveled for it.
* Maybe too much content. In reality, this shouldn't be a complaint. A reasonable person could simply follow the main quest and complete a handful of side quests at their leisure. If you're a completionist, though, beware: you risk getting burned out if you try to do everything.

All in all, this is a fantastic action RPG that deserves a lot more recognition. It's a shame that the studio is done, but maybe with enough support somebody else will pick up the IP and develop a sequel!

I'm not very much into reviewing games and such, but I feel like opening some exceptions occasionally, for games that I really enjoyed and particularly for those that I feel are under appreciated. That is the case of Kingdoms of Amalur. Played it for over 230 hours and I remember thinking a while back, around mid-game, "this game is so awesome, have already 100+ hours played and still feels fresh!".

The gameplay is the secret. With its huge map and option to roam around or fast travel, you can dedicate yourself strictly to the quests, or you can explore and engage in combat whenever you like. And let me tell you, the combat is amazing, with its melee fluidity, mixed with magic powers and potions of all sorts and kinds, all very nicely implemented and presented.

Adding to the variety, you can also dedicate yourself to blacksmithing, alchemy and crafting gems from shards to make even more powerful weapons, you can evolve your character adding points to a set of skills as you level up, like persuasion, lockpicking, detect hidden, stealth, and so on.

Really, there's lots to do, it's a beautiful game, even considering the a bit outdated graphics (but still very nice), and the gameplay is top notch. Being a rather long game, you can feel tired and find it repetitive at times, especially in the dungeons. But even so, overall, it's a very enjoyable game.

The story, context and background are supplied through books and lorestones placed all over Amalur, as well as through contact with the NPCs. You can read it or you can skip it. Myself, I give much importance to the setting in a game and the way the story unfolds, which must be engaging. I use Bioshock and Mass Effect as benchmarks for this. In Amalur, the story is not the most important thing. The setting is rather nice, but the story sometimes unfolds too slowly and a bit confusing. The books and lore bits are often too big and boring. So, some I read, some I didn't. But this didn't hindered me from having a great experience with this game, which I did, including enjoying the story and the lore.

On the downside, like I already wrote, one can feel some repetition as the game goes, especially in the dungeons and also with the NPCs. These are very often variations of the same models. They do have different voices and behavior, which balances the look repetitiveness. Also, the boss battles that sometimes occurs are many times against more powerful variations of the NPCs and this I think could have been better, introducing a few more epic proportion battles, instead of only 2 epic bosses.

This game gets an awful lot of credit as a "hidden gem." It deserves only some of that credit. 
It is hidden (it was released in the shadow of Skyrim), but it's not a gem. It's just a neat rock. 

It's a messy combination of action RPG and MMO (do you like fetch quests?) set in Generic Fantasy World with Generic Fantasy Villains created by the king of Generic Fantasy, R.A. Salvatore. And goofy weapons. In fact, everything looks a little goofy. It's a cartoony aesthetic. 

That said, there's quite a lot to do. There is, of course, a main story quest; there are three factions; and there are numerous side quests. You can technically go wherever you want, but unlike Skyrim, the world doesn't level with you, so you can wander into a zone you're not ready for -- or outlevel the zone your story quests are in. 

Character progression is pretty shallow. There are the three typical class trees -- warrior, mage, rogue -- each with several different weapon types. You can mix and match at will, and if you screw up, you can respec pretty easily. But there's nothing new here, because the class trees are so generic. Rogues are either archers or assassins. Warriors are either tanks or berserkers. Mages are just . . . mages. Your build won't be aimed at specialization, but rather at which combination of class skills you can get away with. 

I do recommend this game, but with the following qualification: If you've played through the big RPGs like Skyrim, Witcher, Dragon Age, etc., and you need something different to play, this game is your answer. I found a nice little niche for it in the rotation while Skyrim is on cooldown. If you're looking for something new and unique, this is not it.

(most of my hours in this game are on Origin, not Steam)

A lot of users compare this game to Skyrim, when really it is more like a single-player mix of Torchlight II and Guild Wars 2. Tons of missions, deep crafting, combo-friendly combat, a huge game-world and genuinely interesting lore means a lot of time can be spent in Amalur. 
Installed size on hard drive (with all DLC): 11.6 GB

Reckoning is rather like a single-player MMO, if that makes any sense. Looting, crafting and leveling are the primary attractions. There is a ton of loot; putting points into the “detect hidden” skill reveals secret rooms and passageways that have even more loot. You'll want to loot as much as you can, even armor sets that you won't use – put points into blacksmithing, disassemble the armor and weapons you don't want to get the parts, and craft something truly epic. Leveling up provides new abilities, new special moves for weapons. At the end of each leveling session, you get to choose a “Fate Card” with special bonuses. Fate Cards are not class-specific, meaning you can use them to create a warrior mage who equips heavy armor, or an archer can wield heavy weapons, or a thief / rogue who also has some magic. There are dozens of hybrid “Fate Cards.” And if you're not happy with how your build has turned out, visit a Fateweaver to “Remix your Fate” and reset your build so you can level up again with your existing points.

The world is huge. There are a lot of places to explore with side-missions hidden everywhere. The graphics are 2012 era DirectX 9: Colorful, bright, and occasionally low-res. The general comic-book style of the artwork hides some graphical shortcomings. And on the plus side, if you have a less-than-stellar gaming PC, the game will probably run just fine. (Back in the day, I ran it on a 1GB Radeon 6670 without issues). The soundtrack by Grant Kirkhope catches the ambiance nicely. The voice acting is generally good (though your hero is silent, a la Dragon Age Origins).

Not everything is excellent, unfortunately. Combat flows well, encouraging the use of different moves. Despite the many different skills and abilities at my disposal, once I found a way to dispose of mobs, I just stuck to that, and never really tried to change up my attacks. I won't say combat is easy – if you go into an area under-leveled, you'll die fast (even with potions). But once you're comfortable in the system, combat becomes just another chore. Fetch quests are repetitive. All exploration is done on foot – no horses. The dungeons are NOT copy / pasted; there's a lot of variety here. But the missions that use the dungeon and cave levels tend to follow similar patterns. If you try to do a completionist run of Reckoning, you'll need a titanic level of patience and dedication. Inventory management, frankly, s*cks. Oh, and jumping. You can't jump, except at prescribed places (“press F to jump”).

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a great game if you love messing about in an open world while worrying about plot later. If you're looking for a go-anywhere, do-anything adventure (with the freedom to jump wherever you want), you'll probably be happier with Skyrim. Or online with friends in Guild Wars 2. Sometimes, though, a solitary, easy grind for loot is exactly what you want - and exactly what Reckoning provides.

On DLC:
The Weapons and Armor DLC provides three complete weapons sets that are accessible at the start of the game. While great to have, the things you craft will quickly surpass them in quality and effectiveness. 

The Teeth of Naros and The Legend of Dead Kel are both large additions to an already massive game. Each provides a new campaign and entirely new areas to explore. Naros in particular is a great piece of DLC. Both have a lot of content in an industry where content-laden DLC are rare. Definitely worth it to get both.

Notes:
An EA account is NOT required. Though the game asks for an EA login on startup, you can simply click the X in the corner to skip the login. The game will play and save normally.

The company that developed Reckoning, 38 Studios, went bankrupt in 2013. The only support for the game is what you will find when trawling the forums.

One of the most underrated games out there. It's a hack and slash style open world RPG, with great gameplay, combat, and graphics for its time. Too bad we can't get a sequel because the devs got bankrupt. 

Also, shoutout to Ellen from outsideextra for introducing this game to the people. 

10/10 would hope for a sequel

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a game that EA has published that is actually good. It is an older game since writing this review so some aspects may seem dated when compared to games like the Witcher 3, however that doesn't mean you should avoid it.

Pros:
+ The game is very well optimized. If you have a somewhat modern system then it should run fine.
+ This game is pretty. It doesn't have the cutting edge graphics of RDR2, but it has a nice vibrant artstyle which makes it visually appealing
+ Decent voice acting. The voice acting is solid, but just like Skyrim you may run into characters with the same voice actor.
+ Unique world and lore. At first the game looks like it's set in a generic fantasy world, but once you meet the Fae you will see that they are an interesting take on the traditional Tolkien elves. The idea of Fate is also a creative way to explain why the player character can behave differently from the NPCs.
+ The class system is fun to mess around with and respec-ing is super easy.
+ Combat is really fun and easy to pick up. It doesn't have the depth that Dark Souls has, but it doesn't need it. It includes combos that are traditionally seen in fighting games.

Cons:
- MMO like quests. Some quests in this game feel like they fit in an MMO more than a single player RPG. This is more of a problem if you play with the completionist mindset because you will be playing through plenty of filler quests.
- Lack of variety in zones. The zones are visually distinct from each other, however there are multiple smaller sections in each zone which will get repetitive.
- Some notable bugs still exist, which may cause some frustration. Like a certain armor set which gets stuck in your inventory if you store it away then put it back in your inventory.
- Low enemy variety. You will see many of the same enemy types throughout the entirety of the game.
- This game is on the easier side. Deaths will be rare and when you do die it may feel like the game cheated you.

I may update this review if I can think of other pros and cons for Amalur.

This is one of those games that you either love or hate.  Gameplay-wise, it's quite reminiscent of the Elder Scrolls series with a Fable style feel to the graphics.  Yeah, the landscapes and denizens are remarkably clean for an agrarian based society and it's a pig to mod but there's something inherently fun about running around a huge, open landscape weilding weapons that, in many cases, are bigger than you are.

As a lower level character there are plenty of loot drops to enable you to afford the healing, training and equipment that you're going to need to progress through the game and the merchants have unlimited funds to buy the plethora of weapons, armour and potions that are simply beneath you to use.  The real challenge is in levelling your character to the point where the abilities and skills you choose complement your gameplay style rather than feel like an adjunct.  The ability to visit a fateweaver and pay them to be able to reset all your skill & ability points is a plus...if you're unhappy with the skill trees you've chosen or if they're just not working for you...change 'em.  It's all about experimenting to find the style of combat (might, finesse, sorcery or a mixture of two or all three) that provides you with the most enjoyable playing experience.

There are plenty of dialogue options that allow you to choose the essential nature of your character...good, evil or indifferent although the opportunites to be a really nasty Dark Lord style world destroyer are too few and far between for my liking...what's the point of making a pact with a Niskaru Lord when it doesn't give you any visible benefits other than having Warsworn mercenaries trying to kill you at every turn?

The world itself is open - always a plus - and the addition of the two DLCs will allow you to run around like a headless chicken for weeks, slaughtering anything you come across that's weaker than you and getting squashed like a bug by trolls and niskaru...at least until you've got to level 20 or above at which point, you'll want to move to hard difficulty if you haven't already because it starts to get a little too easy.

Side quests are plentiful and, in many cases, are more fun than the main mission.  Plenty of faction quests too, most of which are advanced tutorials in the different styles of gameplay and the careful choice of abilities & skills which is where a visit to the fateweaver to change your point allocations is a must.

All in all this game is fun to play and is one you can happily drop for a couple of weeks and then come back to without having to remember how to play it again.  It's challenging enough to keep you engrossed yet not difficult enough to be frustrating and the control and combat systems are simple to understand and use.  Voice acting is good, graphics are bright, colourful and well rendered and, despite some truly ugly or stupid looking armour sets there's not really anything negative to say about this game.  Buy it, play it, enjoy it...but tackle the DLCs [i]after[/i] you finish the main game - you'll need a higher level character to stay alive.

About 114 hours hours in at the time of this review.  

And I haven't tired of the game yet. Somewhat addictive, lol!

First off- it is an "older" game, fairly typical of RPG's of that time. Runs great on my 5+ year old desktop toaster, running  Win7 Pro 64 bit. I have seen some reports of it not running well on new Win10 rigs, but can't confirm what the issues may be. Other than... Windows 10? (Nothing against Windows 10... it just has a ton of issues running older games.)

Graphics are good, clean, crisp, with good animations for the time. The animations are smooth, and look much better than some newer games. No lag, fps issues, stuttering or hitching in my game so far. (Though I will say the game was released just before my rig was built, so the system specs I have may just be "perfect" for what the game was made to run on.)

4 Races to choose from, great customization for character appearance (cosmetics only), Destinies (aka/Classes) are slightly limited, but you can choose to mix 1, 2 or all 3 Destinies together by applying Lvl Up points to the respective skill trees. Only 1 point per Lvl Up for specialities... think carefully before applying that single point. Specialities give buffs to certain abilities, some are rather unneccessary to level up IMO. (Mercantile... gold is a bit scarce at the beginning, but it won't be for long.) Your Destinies (or Fates) cards give buffs as well, and you can switch them around, but only when you Lvl Up.

Combat is really fun. Not too hard, but not too easy either. Enemy types range from monsters with different attacks and buffs and weapons, to humans. Some are easy to kill, some are a real B**ch. Some weapons seem OP- Chakrams were supposed to be too OP according to other reviewers and folks on the forums. I chose a Mage/Warrior mix, with Greatsword/Longsword and Staves/Scepters. I can use any weapon I choose, but the ones I chose to level up in the skill trees give me buffs, while the ones I did not give only simple dps. (Also keep in mind you can find a Fateweaver at certain loactions onn the maps, and pay gold to to respec your character's weapons skills, spells and such, change Destinies. So don't panic if your build seems bad, find a Fateweaver, smash destroyable props to collect more gold, or sell off excess inventory for gold o to pay the Fateweaver. The fee is quite reasonable, all things considered.)

You have to make choices. Some choices will haunt you. (Like stealing from the Vorms... and killing them and the NPC there that I had a side quest for... failed because I did not turn it in before killing them.) You can lose some valuable or not-so-valuable quest rewards based on choices you make. I would redo that one, lol. (I lost a merchant location by having to kill them... don't steal from merchant facilities, lol!)

The story is good, it has enough depth to make me want to keep going, to see where it leads. Some choices you make in dialogue exchanges seem to change the course of the story as well. The map is HUGE, even without the DLC's. (I have not even touched the DLC's yet...). Lots of nods to mythology and historical lore and well known fables or stories. Some are factual history that has been altered a bit to fit the game's story, but it all fits and worls well together. 

Quests/sidequests... you will be smothered in quest objective markers on the mini-map. Up to you if you want to take every side quest offered. Some are very long and somewhat drawn out for the meager rewards you earn. Some are faster and reward you quite handsomely. Some, (Tasks) can be neverending and are simply a way to earn fast gold for your character. No clue if skipping some of the side quests affects the story and game progression. The Main Story quests seem to be the ones you MUST complete.

A definite buy, perhaps best on a deep discount, as the dev studio that made the game went under some time ago, so there will likely never be a sequel made. (Which is a crying shame... I can see so many branching paths that could make for good lead-ins to a sequel...). So your purchase is only going to support the publisher (whom many of us have mixed feelings about). Keep an eye out for sales here and on bundle sites. If you missed it in the Steam Halloween Sale, it will likely come up on deep discount again soon. And at 144 hours so far, seeing many more to come (only 2/3 of the base game maps explored, lol), it was worth it to me to get this game.

As far as replayability, IMHO, there is some, trying out new Races and Destinies, seeing if different choices in specialities, weapons and dialogue choices make a real difference, and completing different side quests and tasks that you skipped in a previous playthrough. I'll let you know about that when I start a second run, in a few hundred more game hours. (You can only have 1 character going, no ability to start a second game with a new characte, without manually copying and moving save files around.) You can save the game frequently (and you should), to go backwards and restart a quest or try to get all achievements in one game. Don't lose track of where you saved and why though... having dozens of self-made checkpoints is great, until you realize 6 of them are labeled with the same town or location, and you don't know which one to choose to go for that achievement.

I like it. I am saddened that the dev studio that made it is gone. And that the game never seemed to get the attention of gamers like I feel it should have. (Which is why I am first playing it almost 6 years after it's release... I never knew about it until I saw a friend's screenshots.). Great older RPG, more open-world than many, more choices you can make to create a more unique playthrough for yourself.

A very underated RPG that is often forgotton about with one of the best combat systems in any fantasy RPG,while not  a true open world it is still extremely expansive with loads of content and a must play for fans of Fantasy RPGs.

This is a review that's going to make me very sad. A sad tiger is not a sight people should have to witness, but nonetheless, hear the tale of the tigers' lament. Hear the tale of the RPG that once was, and will never be. The tale of Amalur.

Kingdoms of Amalur was pitched as a wide, sprawling, epic world. Written by R. A. Salvatore and artwork by Todd McFarlane, this was a world where big names came together to produce an impressive, colourful vista. One where grand battles were fought, where the history of races was told in rich tapestries and stories of lore. Where gnomes were no longer the comedy option (World of Warcraft, yes, you, stop hiding in the back there, this is you I speak to at this point!). A world where the strings of fate invisibly guided everything and everyone around them, and those who could read the weave could fortell glimpses of the future.

The story revolves around the antagonist, one who has managed to unpick the very threads of fate, and the protaganist, you, similarly freed from fate, and your journey from the rags on your back (and the start which sees you unceremoniously dumped in a pile or corpses), to eventual confrontation with the evil that threatens to consume the world. The story has been told many times in many other games, but it is presented with a style and sheen that carries itself well here, the core plot quests keep a coherency and pace that maintain your interest through the rather lengthy world. Not to mention the absolute *ton* of side quests and factions you can involve yourself in, and their own stories and backgrounds, all of which are intricately details and have their own little plot twists. This is a game that prides itself on depth.

... Right up until you step into it and realise that this was probably intended as an MMO. It... takes a bit of a mental adjustment to begin with, because the world, and everything in and around it, feels at first -like- an MMO made singleplayer, there's the vendors, the towns, the crafting system, in fact, so little of it feels single player tailored you'd be forgiven for asking "Where are all the other players?". Once you begin the combat however, that slowly fades into the background, combat in the game is intuitive, flashy, and visceral, with a wide variety of weapons, and a constant encouragement to alternate between magic and weapon attacks, this is a game that rewards variety and creative use of your toolset.

Get over that initial mental bump however, and you'll quickly settle into a large, expansive game, with a wide and diverse world, which okay, will oft remind you that it does feel like an MMO minus the other players, but then equally it will take you places and on journeys that a lot of Roleplaying games have almost forgotten how to manage these days. It's a wonderful thing.

This unfortunately is why I am a sad tiger. The company that made this game is now bankrupt, and the assets have been sold off and everything connected to it, scattered to the four winds. There will not be a sequel, or an MMO, or any further patches or adjustments. The final product is what you get here, with a few idiosyncracies and all. It is a flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless. If you wish to get lost in a world for a few days and embark on a properly epic journey, visiting Amalur is definitely a place to consider.

Kingdoms of Amalur: The Reckoning is so fantastical that it may as well have been written by R.A. Salvatore. 

Oh wait...It was?  Oh, okay. 

You start the game as a corpse, being corpsey on top of a big ol' corpse pile. Frankly at this point you're just happy to have company. But suddenly you wake up and you're no longer a corpse. Disheartened, you leave the pile and set off on an adventure. A very, very long adventure. 

Kingdoms of Amalur is a fast paced, action RPG based more around dodging, blocking, and combos then it is stats and things like status effects. Instead of choosing a class at the beginning of the game you instead choose your class depending on what you put your points into. For example, putting all your points into Might unlocks nothing but warrior classes, all your points into finesse makes you a super good rogue, and all points into magic makes you a giga wizard. 
Or you can mix it up and instead get a class card that's a mix of two or even all three class types. So yes, you can build Might and Magic and create a muscle wizard. 

Combat is fairly arcadey and fast pace, you still do damage depending on your stats, but I haven't found an enemy you couldn't take out at any level if you were good enough. You can equip two weapons, a primary and secondary weapon, and can switch in between them freely. This leads to opportunities to extend combos and maximize damage as well as adding whatever spells or powers you have on your character for some ludicrous Devil May Cry looking stuff. 
It also gives you an opportunity to counter an enemy attack instead of blocking or dodging, since human enemies usually go into a stun animation when you hit them, while you need to start dealing some damage on larger foes before they start to waver.

So if someone is readying an attack, you can switch to your faster weapon and cut them off instead of dodging or blocking/parrying. It's actually really neat just how many combat options they managed to fit into this game. 

I would suggest playing on hard, however. Even normal difficulty is far too easy unless you're looking for the most casual experience possible. But at that point just. You know, watch a movie.

INTRODUCTION

I own Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning on PS3 and PC with all the DLC for both.  I'm on my 6th time through the game, but the first time on PC.  Here is a quick rundown of the game.


STORY

The story was written by New York Times bestselling author R.A. Salvatore, as a side-note. The main storyline keeps your interest, although many of the side quests are common bounty or fetch quests.  The storyline concerning the Summer and Winter Fae is probably the most interesting.  Even though I played through the fairly linear storyline before, I still love the game.  It takes a couple times through just to absorb the whole story really.  There are alot of extras about the background of this world.  I do wish more races would have been included in the storyline to allow for more choices than 4 for the player to choose from.  However, this lack of races is overshadowed by the quality of classes or skill combinations you can create.

I will add that I absolutely love the Dead Kel DLC.  It allows you to have your own island fortress that is upgradeable. For those who like crafting, or sandbox games, this is as close as you get to having an RPG / adventure game with some open-world elements mixed in.  


GRAPHICS

Not the newest graphical achievements in the industry, but well suited to the game's core purpose.  Similar in style to World of Warcraft, but with its own uniqueness.  The colors are vibrant and the world is interesting.  Each area, or region, has its own tone and looks really good.  I know there are better graphical games today, but this one still has a charm all its own.  The races and different NPCs are interesting enough to make the game varied in this detail.  Looks good but doesn't require a great rig to run it.  


SOUND

The music and sound effects in this game are intriguing.  There are records of the Fae, which continually give back story throughout your travels.  This alone constantly reminds me the story was written by a successful novelist.  Great ambient sound effects in each region, memorable battle music and affectual cut scene music.  Everything goes well to set the mood and carry the story.  Also, there has been a lot of thought to how the SFX of menus, items, weapons, etc., all work together.  Some sounds, like the sound of arrows being reloaded to your quiver, are integral to knowing how to proceed in combat without having to actually lookup and see the arrow icons in your HUD.  


GAMEPLAY

The combat is very satisfying.  One thing that makes this game different from many other RPGs is the fact that combat often relies on quick reflexes.  The use of your skills can be so rewarding because there is a learning curve involved.  Although you can complete this game without being super good at dodging, rolling, slinging, swinging, casting, etc., the full potential of becoming really good with your class build is available.  The less hardcore players could still be fine using potions to make it through the tougher fights.  Nothing beats slaying a troll with a variety of attacks without taking a single hit.  

This is my first play with mouse and keyboard and so far it's still fun. It is different with a controller but still another type of fun with keyboard and mouse.  


INTERFACE

The menus are what you would expect from other RPG games.  I do like how each new armor, weapon, item, consumable, etc, is starred to let you know you just picked it up.  Although, this will cost you a bit of extra time clearing them as well.  There is a quick-item radial menu that you can bind consumables to.  I don't like how the quests don't have floating text to follow.  They have an icon on the mini-map but no summary of the quest visible as you run around tracking a particular quest.


SUMMARY

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a hidden gem because of its incredible storyline, settings, sound and gameplay. This game has decent replayability because that itch for quick and rewarding combat will need to be scratched often.  
There have been some attempts lately at giving RPG games more exciting combat, this game accomplished it long ago.

And the cartoonish style is actually very beautiful, when you give it a closer look! The variety of landscapes and details – just exploring the game's world is rewarding on its own. (Take a look at my screenshots and you'll know what I'm talking about).

I believe it would be fair to say that, "Kingdoms of Amalur" is "Skyrim meets Mass Effect"... just without sexy lesbian shower scenes... and without choices that actually matter. 

Well, about that... Choices - this aspect is actually one of the minor faults of this game. It gives the impression that you have to make moral choices that will affect your future, but (apart from few barely significant exceptions in some of the side quests) all those choices change is, whether you accept a sidequest and how the NPCs answer you. They don't affect the main storyline and don't lead to alternative endings - there are no alternative endings. On the other hand, you won't be regretting anything and wishing that you had done something differently.

Especially because you can change your class (!) at any point in the game and redistribute your skills and abilities ("skills" are boosts to your stats in this game and "abilities" are your class-specific skills). And, in this aspect, KoAR is rather unique. There are 3 traditional classes in this game: rogue, warrior and mage. Also, you can combine any two of them or all three of them. This system reminds me that of Mass Effect. The only difference is that your choice is not fixed in the beginning, but you specialise your character in one of the three directions with each next level.

What else? Loot. There's a lot of it! But only few items are actually worth something - as always in this type of games! But, contrary to Borderlands, for example, you won't be spending as much time sorting your inventory. Just put everything you don't need to junk right away. Then you can sell it or salvage to craft new items.

Crafting, exploring, potion brewing, lore stone searching (they grant stat boosts), side quests, faction quests (they grant valuable rewards in the form of cards), appearance customisation, improvement of your headquarters – there is really a lot of content in this game. And that might feel overwhelming sometimes. You just grow tired of this game, especially because at one point this game stops being challenging even on the hardest difficulty. And the enemies and battles start to feel the same. You just want to find out how everything ends. But it just doesn't. This game takes for what feels like an eternity.

My suggestion is to take breaks from time to time. Thus, when you return to it, it will still feel fresh.

Don't ruin the experience for yourself! Because the story is rich and interesting, the combat system is versatile, the skill trees are complex, the numerous kingdoms of Amalur are beautiful, the sidequests are unique (well, most of them), there are various factions of enemies and the game itself offers immersive fantasy adventure experience that will take you hours to complete.

If only the graphics were more realistic, the enemies were more challenging towards the end and there was no level cap (=40), this would have been the perfect game for me.

Nevertheless, 10 EUR well spent.

The game places you in the role of the “Fateless One”, a mysterious character who was recently resurrected back from the dead and discovers a new found power to change destiny itself. Travel the land of Amalur in search of answers on why you were recalled back into the land of the living and at the same time, learn more about a great war in the east against an immortal race called the Tuatha Deohn and why they want you dead...again.

Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning

Kingdoms of Amalur Reckoning feels like a game from a very different time. A very specific time particularly the PS 2 era which I think is a great era for PC games as well. Where experimentation is rewarded with a fun gameplay loop and if you want a story is there somewhere. And boy does this game delivers at times with some impressive experimentation on the action role playing (ARPG) genre. It has some similar Diablo like pull factor with loot but plays a bit like the old God of War (GoW) games meets Neverwinter Nights quest moments. In one sense it feels like a bunch of games combine into one but don’t be fool this game does have a personality of its own. 

Develop by the now defunct 38 studios and the still existing big huge games, Kingdoms of Amalur has a rather unique world that sets itself apart from most common high fantasy setting. It holds much more similarity to Nickelodeon’s Avatar series instead, with the immortal races of the Fae and other mortal races (humans, elves, and gnomes to name but a few) living in regions designated by the seasons which I thought was unique. This is the simplest way to explain it but its more complex than that obviously.
 
The story is not anything groundbreaking but the world and its lore is interesting. Although it follows the usual chosen one story trope to the letter, it differs somewhat with the lore’s emphasis on fate and this bit is actually quite fascinating. The concept of believing of ones predetermined path from the get go and not questioning it poses some interesting themes as well as questions but sadly goes unanswered as the game continues. The game also has tons of personality with each of the regions having their own history, towns, cities, politics, lorestones and different eco system. There are some pretty cool side quest but poor supporting and generic characters kind of sour the experience somewhat. This is not help by a rather monotonous voicework and delivery as well as generic fetch quests. It’s kind of a miss opportunity sadly with all that lore by R.A Salvatore and his team. There are also dialog options but to be honest does not really change the outcome that much. However the story does pull you in somewhat despite being delivered poorly in terms of voice acting and plot predictability. 

The game play’s wonderfully though despite the generic main campaign and there are stand out moments. The Battle of Mal Senshir to name but a few. The attack combos are remarkably fun to use. Using the Chakrams, a rather unique weapon that looks like some magical ballet thing are some of the biggest highlight for me. I like the fact that the game also feels comfortable on a keyboard too where most ARPG’s are more comfortable with a controller. Switching back and forth between your two chosen weapons is smooth and easy with the Q button next to your standard directional buttons. Using the spells are also pretty smooth. There is also a power move you can use or reckoning mode which slows down the enemies and allows you to do fatalities on your enemies. Using this mode strategically allows you to collect more experience too. The loot was also not too bad as well.  The biggest highlight though is experimenting with the game’s unique destiny system that is tied to your class system. Want a combination of thief and warrior. You can do that and get some bonus perk with critical damage. Prefer thief and sorcery, you get to upgrade your dodge ability to some cool mini teleporting or blink. The experimentation is quite huge and fun. Finishing various side quest line also unlock more perks by adding more destiny cards. I think that is what it’s called.

However the game does get fairly easy and like most open world games, it falls into that trap of giving you a ton of random chore like fetch quest which is a shame. While there are a ton of various unique enemies, they do get recycle a bit. Different regions, different colored enemies that sort of thing. There are some terrific boss moments and cool dungeons design at first but their design layout gets repeated a lot in the later stages. The graphics is nothing to shout about but as mention earlier it does have a ton of personality. The forest like autumn areas of Dalentarh exhumes serene like moments while the swampy swamps of Klurikon oozes mystery and dread. Colours pop out like something from WoW but it’s also uniquely its own game. Generally I thought the game was very pretty to look at despite its age. The music however gets very repetitive and has your standard high fantasy orchestral moments.

This game sometimes embodies the phrase diamond in the rough to the letter emphasizing if it had more time it could have been a great ARPG but to me to some extent it is a great game because I had a lot fun just playing it. The two DLC’s also have some pretty neat story ideas more than the campaign especially with Teeth of Naros. The game is also a steal as it is being price really low. Despite the lackluster by the numbers story, I had tremendous fun using my chakrams, experimenting, exploring its many ballads and lore of the Faelands.

Gameplay – 9 I had a lot of fun with its combat loop 
Sound – 5 Poor voice delivery and repeated ost
Story – 6 Standard chosen one story and felt like a missed opportunity with its lore
